disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features is characterized by at least one manic episode of sufficient intensity to cause marked impairment, often requiring hospitalization, and may include psychotic symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations that are typically mood-congruent. Manic episodes involve a sustained period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy and goal-directed activity, often accompanied by decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and impaired judgment. The course is usually recurrent, with episodes of mania and, in many patients, major depression, and symptoms may be exacerbated by sleep disruption, psychosocial stressors, or substance use. It is distinguished from schizoaffective or primary psychotic disorders by the temporal relationship between mood episodes and psychosis, and from Bipolar II by the presence of full manic episodes rather than hypomania.

narrative.personality: Michael is a competitive, socially engaged plant supervisor who prides himself on being laid-back and flexible while thriving on activity, teamwork, and community involvement.
narrative.stressor: In the months leading up to his episode, Michael’s plant was acquired by a larger corporation, and he was suddenly tasked with leading a major transition to new production software, stricter quotas, and revamped safety protocols, all under intense scrutiny from new management. Wanting to prove himself and protect his crew, he began stretching his workdays, bringing his supervisory mindset into every corner of his life—constantly checking production data on his phone, volunteering for extra shifts, and taking on multiple improvement projects at once, while still trying to keep up with his basketball league, hunting trips, and community barbecues. The mounting pressure, chronic sleep curtailment, and sense that this was his chance to “make his mark” led him to push beyond his usual easygoing boundaries, becoming increasingly driven, overcommitted, and unable to switch off, with work ideas spilling over into late nights and weekends. Over about two months, his behavior became so dominated by nonstop project planning and hyper-focused initiatives—both at the plant and at home—that he began clashing with management and family, making risky decisions on the shop floor, and finally was sent to occupational health and then to psychiatric care after HR and his brother noticed that his nonstop energy and ambitious schemes were clearly impairing his judgment and job performance.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just can’t slow down—I’ve been going nonstop with a million projects and I feel like I have endless energy.”

narrative.personality: Xiaobing is a calm, reflective construction supervisor with a deep appreciation for art and philosophy, who values harmony and aesthetics but can be laid-back and somewhat disorganized about practical obligations.
narrative.stressor: Around his 50th birthday, Xiaobing found himself at a crossroads: his children were becoming independent, his company was encouraging him to move into a more administrative role, and he had just completed a long-anticipated certification in sustainable building design. This convergence stirred a sense that he was entering a new chapter and needed to redefine his legacy, leading him to dramatically scale back sleep so he could sketch ambitious eco-friendly housing concepts at night, oversee complex jobs by day, and still maintain his hiking, photography, and community volunteer builds. What began as an inspired period of creativity and renewed purpose slowly tipped into an increasingly expansive, driven state in which he felt compelled to champion grand community construction projects, take on multiple volunteer commitments, and insist on incorporating elaborate artistic and cultural elements into routine builds regardless of budget or feasibility. As his ideas grew more grandiose and his mood more labile—swinging from intensely elevated, visionary enthusiasm to sharp irritability when others questioned him—his work relationships deteriorated, project schedules slipped, and his spouse and foreman jointly urged him into psychiatric evaluation after he disrupted several job sites and became convinced that only he could “see” the true, higher design of their town.
narrative.chief_complaint: “For weeks I’ve felt unusually ‘up’ and on edge at the same time, like I’m on a mission and everyone is getting in my way.”

narrative.personality: Leslie is a highly organized, competitive young production worker who relies on meticulous planning and structure, yet occasionally channels that intensity into obsessive projects and impulsive hobby splurges.
narrative.stressor: Leslie’s episode emerged after a period of escalating pressure at work coincided with her decision to take extra online coursework toward Lean Six Sigma certification while still working full-time on rotating shifts. Determined to prove herself as promotion-ready despite being younger than most colleagues, she began stacking her schedule with overtime, exam preparation, and side projects to “fix” inefficiencies on the production line, cutting back on sleep and rigidly tracking every hour in spreadsheets. What initially felt like a productive, high-achieving phase gradually shifted into an increasingly driven, tense state in which she filled evenings and nights with elaborate process maps, meal-prep marathons, and intricate model-building, becoming more impatient and combative with coworkers and family whenever they questioned her pace or priorities. Over roughly two months, her relentless activity, escalating irritability when interrupted, and inability to disengage from new goals led to serious conflict on the floor, missed safety steps, and academic difficulties; after a shouting match with a supervisor and a near-miss incident at work, HR and her parents insisted she see a psychiatrist because her normally controlled, methodical demeanor had transformed into nonstop, agitated overdrive that was clearly undermining her functioning.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve been stuck in this wired, irritable overdrive for weeks, like I can’t stop doing things and everyone is setting me off.”
